niﬁcant tetraparesis, and patient completed inpatient rehabilitation.
At 4 months post-injury, patient had nearly full strength throughout
with the exception of 3/5 strength in the distal left upper extremity.
Patient’s pain was managed with buprenorphine patch and gaba-
pentin. Over the next 7 months, distal left upper extremity symptoms
progressively worsened, and patient presented to orthopedics for
ongoing left forearm burning pain and left intrinsic hand weakness.
Examination was notable for extensor weakness in the left wrist,
digits, and thumb. Sensation and reﬂexes were intact. Hoffman’s was
negative. Diagnostic MRI of the cervical spine was negative for new
signiﬁcant lesions.
Setting: Tertiary care hospital system.
Results: Electrodiagnostic studies were obtained showing left poste-
rior interosseous neuropathy based on active denervation with poly-
phasic potentials in PIN muscles. The patient underwent PIN neurolysis
to relieve pain and potentially improve function. During surgery, the
patient was found to have signiﬁcant compression at the arcade of
Frohse. The patient is currently enrolled in outpatient physical ther-
apy to address functional goals.
Discussion: In individuals with central cord syndrome and polytrauma,
it may be difﬁcult to distinguish new versus premorbid pathology when
evaluating persistent pain and weakness, especially in the upper ex-
tremities. Electrodiagnostic evaluation can be a critical tool in local-
izing lesions and guiding management.
Conclusions: Peripheral nerve lesions should be considered in in-
dividuals with spinal cord injuries with ongoing pain and weakness
which is not explained by central pathology.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 261:
Coexistent Spasticity and Hemi-Body Tonic Spasms in a
Patient with Spinal Cord Injury Secondary to
Neuromyelitis Optica
Ashley MF . Johnson, MD (Temple University Hospital, Philadelphia,
PA, United States), Marlyn Ramos Lamboy, MD
Disclosures: Ashley Johnson: I Have No Relevant Financial Relation-
ships To Disclose
Case/Program Description: A 23-year-old woman with newly diag-
nosed neuromyelitis optica (NMO) who presents with poorly controlled
spasms.
Setting: Spinal Cord Unit-Acute Inpatient Rehabilitation (AIR).
Results: This is the case of a 23-year-old woman who initially pre-
sented with vomiting, nausea and progressive weakness 1 month
post-partum. Laboratory studies and imaging suggested a diagnosis of
NMO. Her weakness progressed to tetraplegia, and she presented to
AIR with a C1 AIS C spinal cord injury. The patient’s hospital course
was complicated by poorly controlled spasticity. She had already
been maximized on baclofen. During her ﬁrst week at AIR, tizanidine
was added and slowly titrated. She underwent medical workup to
rule out the most common causes of spasticity exacerbation. Brain
and cervical spine MRI were obtained to evaluate the presence of
acute demyelination, but imaging was negative. During repeat
physical examination, a painful sustained increased muscle tone with
abnormal posturing of the left side of her body was observed,
consistent with paroxysmal hemi-body tonic spasms (PHTS). The pa-
tient was treated with carbamazepine which was effective in con-
trolling her spasms. Tizanidine continued to be titrated for spasticity
control. Concomitant treatment of spasticity and spasms allowed for
consistent participation in therapies, reduced pain and improved

quality of life.
Discussion: PHTS is not commonly seen in the usual spinal cord injury
population, where most tone is attributed to spasticity. Lack of fa-
miliarity with the association of tonic spasms with NMO can lead to
diagnostic difﬁculty. Furthermore, spasticity and PHTS may co-exist,
making diagnosis more challenging.
Conclusions: Clinicians should be familiar with diagnosis and man-
agement of PHTS, a potential sequela of NMO, which deceptively re-
sembles spasticity. Daily physical evaluations are instrumental for
appropriate diagnosis. Carbamazepine is a viable treatment option for
PHTS.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 262:
Acute Inpatient Rehabilitation of Individual Status Post
Orthotopic Heart Transplant who also has Neurologic
Deﬁcits Secondary to Stroke: A Case Report
Nicole Brand, MD (Temple University Hospital/Moss Rehabilitation,
Philadelphia, PA, United States), Ning Cao, MD
Disclosures: Nicole Brand: I Have No Relevant Financial Relationships
To Disclose
Case/Program Description: A 66-year-old man who underwent
orthotopic cardiac transplant. Patient sustained large right middle
cerebral artery hemorrhagic stroke on post-operative day 7. Acute
care hospital course also complicated by dysphagia requiring percu-
taneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube placement, right upper ex-
tremity deep vein thrombosis for which he was started on Eliquis and
pseudomonal urinary tract infection requiring long term intravenous
antibiotics for which peripherally inserted central catheter was placed
in left upper extremity. Patient was transferred to acute inpatient
rehabilitation hospital. On admission was found to have deﬁcits
including left neglect and hemiparesis, decreased sitting balance,
cognition, and activity tolerance, moderate oropharyngeal dysphagia,
moderate deﬁcits in auditory comprehension, limited non-ﬂuent
speech, impulsivity and distractibility. Acute inpatient rehabilitation
stay was complicated by left upper extremity deep vein thrombosis
and elevated blood pressure and heart rate during therapy.
Setting: Acute inpatient rehabilitation hospital
Results: Patient completed course of acute inpatient rehabilitation.
On discharge patient was noted to have progressed in functionality, he
was able to initiate unsupported sitting balance for 20-30 seconds,
assist in upper extremity dressing, perform forward leaning at minimal
assistance with verbal cues, assist in two-person total assist transfers,
and showed improved accuracy with multisyllabic word/phrase repe-
tition. He was also able to tolerate diet of chopped consistency with
thin liquids.
Discussion: There is very little literature about the rehabilitation of
individuals with both stroke and cardiac transplant.
Conclusions: Acute inpatient rehabilitation admission is beneﬁcial for
individuals who are post orthotopic cardiac transplant who also have
neurologic deﬁcits secondary to stroke.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 263:
Rehabilitation Challenges in a Rare Combination of Stiff-
Man Syndrome, Cerebellar Ataxia, and Grave’s Disease: A
Case Report
Yulia Rivelis, MD (Monteﬁore Medical Center, New York, NY, United
States), Eathar Saad, MD
Disclosures: Yulia Rivelis: I Have No Relevant Financial Relationships
To Disclose
Case/Program Description: A
 33-year-old woman, diagnosed with
cerebellar ataxia at 23 years old, subsequently diagnosed with Stiff-
man Syndrome at 30 years old. On examination, patient was dysarthric

with otherwise intact cranial nerves. Motor strength was normal with
brisk reﬂexes throughout. Hoffman and Babinski signs were negative
bilaterally. She had ﬁnger-to-nose dysmetria, and positive Romberg.
Gait showed imbalance and lateral sway during tandem walking. Pa-
tient resides with boyfriend who assists with housekeeping. She is in-
dependent with dressing, eating, and transfers.
S87Abstracts / PM R 10 (2018) S1-S128

Setting: University Hospital
Results: Her deﬁcits from a rehabilitation perspective include dysar-
thria, stiff lower extremities, and ataxic gait. Her ambulation and
functionality have improved with physical therapy and monthly IVIG
infusions. She sees speech therapy for dysarthria and dysphonia, and
was referred to seating clinic for a suitable motorized ambulatory
device.
Discussion: Stiff-man syndrome is a rare central nervous system dis-
order characterized by progressive muscle stiffness and spasms. Rarely,
patients later develop cerebellar ataxia. Literature shows that auto-
antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) are implicated in both
conditions and typically present in high serum titers prior to clinical
symptoms. Interestingly, our patient not only developed ataxia prior to
stiffness, but initially had low anti-GAD titers despite already having
symptoms, thus raising suspicion for a genetic component to her ataxia.
However, this was ruled out and titers subsequently increased.
Conclusions: This presentation highlights a rare combination of
Grave’s Disease, Stiff-man Syndrome, and cerebellar ataxia presenting
prior to anti-GAD titers. Our patient is followed by physiatry,
neurology, and is undergoing physical and speech therapy. She faces
difﬁculty performing ADLs, maintaining an exhaustive appointment
list, not to mention the burden placed on her signiﬁcant other, which
takes an emotional and social toll on a young patient. This case em-
phasizes how critical a multidisciplinary approach is for a unique
combination of co-morbidities, making rehabilitation of this patient
that much more difﬁcult.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 264:
Persistent Neurological Deﬁcits After Cerebral Fat
Embolism Despite Negative Neuro Imaging: A Case Report
Abana F . Azariah, MD (Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, Houston,
TX, United States), Haresh Sampathkumar, MD, Bonny S. Wong, MD,
Katherine O’Brien, PhD, Sheng Li, MD, PhD, FAAPMR, Sunil Kothari,
MD, FAAPMR
Disclosures: Abana Azariah: I Have No Relevant Financial Relation-
ships To Disclose
Case/Program Description: A 25-year-old woman sustained poly-
trauma in a motor vehicle collision. Glasgow Coma Scale was 15 with
no loss of consciousness. Physical examination revealed no neurolog-
ical deﬁcits and computed tomography (CT) head was without ab-
normalities. She was diagnosed with right femoral shaft and left
olecranon fractures and underwent intramedullary nailing of the right
femur and open reduction and internal ﬁxation of left olecranon. Post-
operatively she developed seizure like activity and became somnolent.
Setting: Tertiary care rehabilitation hospital
Results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain revealed numerous
punctate foci of restricted diffusion and T2 signal abnormality
throughout the white and gray matter, suggestive of cerebral fat
embolism (CFE). She was transferred to a long term acute care hospital
(LTACH) where she demonstrated frequent episodes of confusion,
agitation, and restless behavior. Repeat brain MRI 2 weeks later at the
LTACH did not show any abnormalities. She was transferred to acute
inpatient rehabilitation, approximately 1-month post-injury. She
continued to have neurological deﬁcits, both cognitive and physical.
However admission CT head revealed no abnormalities. During her stay
in rehabilitation, the patient improved physically and cognitively. At
the time of discharge, the patient was at a supervision level for basic

ADLs and mobility; neuropsychological testing showed mild global
impairment of cognition.
Discussion: Although the patient had characteristic clinical and im-
aging ﬁndings of CFE in the acute care setting, subsequent neuro-
imaging was negative, despite persistent neurologic deﬁcits on
admission to inpatient rehabilitation. No other explanation was found
for her deﬁcits and the pattern was consistent with previous reports of
sequelae of CFE.
Conclusions: Clinicians should consider the possibility of CFE in pa-
tients with a history of unexplained persistent neurological impair-
ment after an orthopedic injury even in the absence of subacute or
late ﬁndings on brain imaging.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 265:
Managing Weakness and Aphasia in a Patient with
Congenital Deafness: A Case Report
Chris J. Lin, MD (Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York
City, NY, United States), Andrew Abdou, DO, Kirk Lercher, MD,
FAAPMR
Disclosures: Chris Lin: I Have No Relevant Financial Relationships To
Disclose
Case/Program Description: A 46-year-old congenitally deaf woman
was found to have a left cerebellopontine schwanomma. She under-
went a left suboccipital craniectomy for tumor resection. Her post-
operative course was notable for impairments in balance, left cranial
nerve VII palsy, and left hemiparesis.
Setting: Inpatient Rehabilitation at Academic Center
Results: The patient was admitted to an acute inpatient rehabilita-
tion facility. She was provided a live translator for American Sign
Language (ASL) for a minimum of 7 hours a day and a video telecom-
munication device when a live translator was unavailable. The patient
required the use of both hands to communicate effectively but this
was limited by her left hemiparesis. Additionally, communication was
adversely affected by left facial droop, decreased ﬁne motor skills,
and receptive language deﬁcits.
Discussion: Participation in therapy was limited due to the challenges
with communication. During bimanual tasks, such as utilizing a walker
with ambulation, the patient, at times, was unable to communicate
effectively and the therapy had to be stopped either due to safety or
ineffective teaching of a task. Furthermore, this patient had receptive
and expressive language deﬁcits, which limited her carryover of
learned instructions. Additionally, multiple translators noted that she
was repetitive and perseverative in her communication. However,
neuropsychology and speech therapists had difﬁculty assessing deﬁ-
cits, as most assessment tools were not designed for deaf patients.
The patient was eventually able to adapt her signing hand gestures to
accommodate her left sided weakness. Communication improved with
cues to slow down signing, consistency by utilizing the same trans-
lators, and improvement with her left arm strength.
Conclusions: Congenitally deaf patients are dependent upon their
vision and upper extremities to communicate. It is imperative that
there be adequate rehabilitation assessment tools to assess this pop-
ulation as well as guidelines on communication and approaching
treatment in order to effectively optimize their rehabilitation
program.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 266:
Weakness and Spasm of Lower Limbs as an Unusual
Presentation of West Nile Virus Infection
Cristina M. Kline-Quiroz, DO (Rutgers-NJMS / Kessler Institute for
Rehabilitation, Jersey City, NJ, United States), Mooyeon Oh-Park, MD,
FAAPMR

Disclosures: Cristina Kline-Quiroz: I Have No Relevant Financial Re-
lationships To Disclose
